findings.where: Article specimen, the lecture card at the end of the article ('Streamlining the PPP Process… · Lecture · 23 April 2026', PDF), desktop and phone
findings.fault: This one card stacks four separate treatments: a pale blue fill, a blue hairline border, rounded corners of about 10 px and a wide, soft drop shadow. Nothing else on the page has rounded corners or a shadow. The hero's blue action, the swatches, the photographs and the motion preview are all square-cornered and sit flat. So the card reads as a component from another design system, a glossy app tile, dropped into a quiet editorial page. A hairline border with a wide soft shadow on one resting element, and a coloured border with a coloured fill, are each a doubled signal.
findings.who_objects: The founder judging the tile, and Angélique, who will add these cards for every lecture and paper. The PDF list is meant to be 'the product' in this direction. Its one specimen looks slicker and more 'app' than the serious, flat paper look around it, which goes against the brief's 'refined, never slick'. Every card she adds will repeat the clash.

findings.where: Article specimen title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law' (desktop and phone); also 'Mark's voice' in the Type pair note and 'the photo's' in the palette notes
findings.fault: These apostrophes are straight typewriter ticks, while the article body beside them uses curly quotes (“ ” ‘ ’). The tick is most visible in the article title, which is set at display size in a fine serif. So the same text uses two kinds of punctuation.
findings.who_objects: A reader with an editorial eye, such as Mark himself or a development-bank reader used to well-set journals. A straight tick in a large serif heading looks like unedited web copy. It undercuts the 'legal journal' care the type pair claims, at the one place the article specimen is meant to show finish.
